newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Israel's Netanyahu to talk trade, peace in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu to talk trade, peace in Russia.

text.p: Benjamin Netanyahu, paying his first visit to Moscow since becoming Israel's prime minister nine months ago, will meet Russian leaders on Tuesday to discuss trade links and Russia's role in Middle East peace talks.

Under fire at home and abroad for his troop redeployment plan for the West Bank, the Israeli leader has made clear he wants to focus on bilateral economic issues and he made no comment on the troubled peace process when he arrived in the Russian capital on Monday.

"Israel is prepared to cooperate with Russia economically. We have a great future together," Netanyahu told reporters at the elegant Metropol hotel where he was the dinner guest of Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov on Monday evening.

"Israel is fast becoming the Silicon Valley of the eastern hemisphere. We have more scientists per capita than any other country," he said, adding that many of these scientists were of Russian origin and could be a bridge to greater cooperation.

More than 650,000 Jews have moved to Israel from the former Soviet Union since Moscow flung open the doors to emigration in 1989 in an era of glasnost (openness), and Netanyahu's government includes several prominent former Russians, including former Soviet Jewish dissident Natan Sharansky.
"We have a million people who speak Russian," Netanyahu said on Monday. "That is the greatest concentration outside the former Soviet Union," he added.
Moscow only re-established long-severed ties with Israel in 1991 for the launch of Arab-Israeli peace talks in Madrid co-sponsored by the United States and the then-Soviet Union.
Israeli officials say bilateral trade has jumped from virtually zero five year ago to around $500 million today and say it is expanding fast.
Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, an Arabic speaker with long experience of the Middle East, is keen to revive Moscow's influence in the region, much reduced by Russia's economic woes.

On Tuesday Netanyahu will hold talks with President Boris Yeltsin in the Kremlin at noon (0900 GMT). He will also meet Primakov, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Russian businessmen and members of Moscow's Jewish community.

His 48-hour visit, which coincides with mounting tension between Israeli soldiers and Palestinians on the West Bank, follows a similar trip to Moscow by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat last month.

"It is very good that the Russian leadership meets today with all sides, both with the Israelis and the Arabs. This can only facilitate dialogue and the lowering of tensions in the region," Israel's ambassador to Moscow, Aliza Shenar, told Ekho Moskvy radio on Monday.
In Soviet times Moscow was a strong supporter of Palestinian self-rule, helping to balance Washington's pro-Israel stance.
Israel wants Moscow to use its influence to persuade Syria, one of the Jewish state's arch-enemies, to resume peace talks.
U.S. President Bill Clinton and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak also agreed on Monday during talks in Washington to try to revive the Syrian-Israeli track of the Middle East peace process.
One issue overshadowing Netanyahu's visit to Moscow concerns sales of advanced military technology to Syria and to Iran.
Netanyahu said last week he would press Russia not to help Iran develop ballistic missiles. Ambassador Shenar also touched on this theme during her radio interview.
"Israel is unhappy with the fact that Russia is selling weapons to Iran and cooperating with it in the area of nuclear energy," she said.

Last month the Los Angeles Times said U.S. intelligence reports indicated Russia had given Iran technology for the Russian SS-4 missile, which has a range almost three times greater than that of any missile now in Tehran's arsenal. Moscow denied the report.

The late Yitzhak Rabin made the first visit of an Israeli prime minister to Moscow in 1994. Sharansky, now trade minister, returned in January on his first trip since being freed from a KGB jail and turned over to the West in a 1986 prisoner swap.
